name: Who Profits: Cost Curve Kings
deck: When commodity prices spike, they no longer compress the earnings of integrated giants. Large operators with hedging power and low breakeven costs pass the shock downstream to smaller buyers and consumers who cannot hedge. The cost curve kings—producers with unit costs far below commodity spot prices—capture the upside while everyone else absorbs the risk.
core_bet: The modern commodity system is no longer unified cost absorption. Large producers with pricing power and financial infrastructure have engineered pass-through contracts and hedging that systematically shift commodity risk away from themselves and onto the next layer—smaller operators, converters, consumers. When nitrogen prices surge or cocoa costs spike, the burden lands on farmers, packagers, construction buyers, and households. CF Industries' 2025 earnings of $1.46B (driven by higher average selling prices on tight global nitrogen supply) and Freeport-McMoRan's copper unit costs of $1.97 per pound against realized prices of $6.17 per pound in Q2 2026 prove the mechanism. Those companies do not absorb commodity volatility. They monetize it.

mechanism: Large integrated commodity producers—CF Industries, Glencore, Freeport-McMoRan, ConocoPhillips—have hedging infrastructure, financial depth, and global sourcing flexibility. When commodity prices rise, they either have locked in supply at lower costs or can quickly activate hedges. They then negotiate pass-through clauses with customers one tier down: packagers like Crown Holdings and Mondelez, or downstream converters like Cleveland-Cliffs. The key mechanism is the pass-through lag and the pricing power asymmetry. Fixed-price contracts amplify the whiplash for smaller operators. Cleveland-Cliffs locks 35-40% of flat-rolled steel sales under fixed annual automotive contracts. When material costs spike, the company absorbs the margin hit for the contract term. When prices fall, the automaker holds the contract price fixed and captures the benefit.

CF Industries earned $1.46B in 2025 net earnings, explicitly attributing the result to higher average selling prices on tight global nitrogen supply. Farmers buying nitrogen fertilizer face supply scarcity; CF passes no pass-through to farmers because fertilizer contracts are structured as take-it-or-leave-it at CF's posted price. Mondelez faced unprecedented cocoa cost headwinds in 2025, forcing organic revenue growth to settle at only 4.3% despite higher selling prices—the company passed costs downstream to retailers and consumers, who faced higher shelf prices for Oreo and Cadbury products. Glencore's H1 2026 marketing adjusted EBIT rose to $3.3B, up 142% year over year. CEO explicitly cited Middle East conflict benefits: the company positioned itself as a trader who profits from supply disruptions rather than as a pure producer absorbing them. This is the transfer mechanism in action: large operators with hedging infrastructure extract value from volatility; smaller operators and end buyers absorb the shocks.

Freeport-McMoRan exemplifies the cost-curve king dynamic. Unit net cash costs of $1.97 per pound copper (Q2 2026) against realized prices of $6.17 per pound create a 313% spread. That spread reflects the company's position at the bottom of the cost curve. Byproduct economics from gold and molybdenum provide additional cushion. Producers at this cost level capture the upside from commodity price spikes while upstream and downstream participants take the downside. Downstream converters like Cleveland-Cliffs cannot hedge against commodity volatility in the same way: fixed annual automotive contracts lock pricing while material costs move daily. The company reported a $1.4B GAAP net loss in 2025, partly driven by the lag between fixed contract pricing and rising material costs. That is the whiplash in action.
why_now: Post-2022 commodity volatility never fully settled. Geopolitical disruptions remain endemic: Iran-related fertilizer supply fragility, Middle East energy conflicts, DRC cobalt production quotas, Indonesian mining regulations. CF Industries explicitly described tight global nitrogen supply and how Iran-related disruption exposed fertilizer supply fragility. Glencore's CEO linked marketing profits directly to Middle East conflict monetization. These are not one-time shocks; they are structural supply scarcities that keep getting extended. Simultaneously, companies have had two years (2024-2026) to harden their pass-through contract infrastructure. CF's 2025 earnings of $1.46B and Glencore's H1 2026 marketing EBIT of $3.3B (up 142%) both arrived in rapid succession in early 2026, proving that large operators have institutionalized the transfer mechanism. The whiplash is no longer random; it is systematic.
who_pays: Farmers buying nitrogen fertilizer. When CF Industries earnings surge on tight nitrogen markets, farmers absorb higher fertilizer costs and adjust acreage or yields downward. Consumers buying packaged treats and beverages. When Mondelez faces unprecedented cocoa cost headwinds (2025), it passes price increases downstream; consumers see higher Oreo and Cadbury prices and buy fewer units. Construction contractors and automotive makers buying finished steel. When Cleveland-Cliffs' materials costs rise faster than fixed contracts allow, the company absorbs the loss temporarily, eventually forcing price renegotiation that hits the OEM's supply chain. Small converters and packagers without hedging infrastructure absorb price shocks directly.
who_profits: Integrated commodity producers with low breakeven costs and hedging infrastructure: CF Industries (nitrogen), ConocoPhillips (oil and gas), Suncor (oil sands), Freeport-McMoRan (copper—unit costs $1.97/lb while realized prices $6.17/lb in Q2 2026). Commodity traders with physical assets and marketing arms. Glencore's H1 2026 marketing EBIT of $3.3B (up 142%) proves that traders who monetize supply disruptions profit more than pure producers. Any operator with pricing power strong enough to pass increases downstream faster than cost inflation arrives extracts value.
tension: Consumer affordability breaks the chain. Mondelez showed that when commodity pass-through hits the shelf price, volume declines. Organic net revenue grew only 4.3% in 2025 despite higher selling prices—the growth was anchored by pricing, not volume. At some price point, the consumer cannot absorb more. They trade down, buy fewer units, or switch to cheaper brands. When volume collapses, the entire margin structure inverts. The most vulnerable operators—those without hedging, without long-term contracts, without scale—bear the full volatility in both directions.
surprising_part: Commodity whiplash is no longer a problem that integrated companies absorb together. Large operators have engineered systematic transfer of volatility to smaller operators while protecting their own margins. Cleveland-Cliffs' fixed-price contracts are the clearest proof: the company does not just fail to capture upside; it actively absorbs downside in ways its customers avoid. Freeport-McMoRan holds 313% margin spread on copper (unit costs $1.97/lb against $6.17/lb realized price), while downstream buyers face cost shocks with no hedging infrastructure. Glencore's marketing business grew 142% year over year in H1 2026 by explicitly monetizing supply disruptions. The system has inverted: commodity risk concentration is now highest among those least able to hedge.
one_sentence: Commodity price swings no longer hit integrated producers—they are systematically passed downstream to smaller operators, converters, and consumers, concentrating financial risk among those with the least ability to hedge.
societal_stake: The companies with the most sophisticated financial infrastructure bear the least commodity risk. The people with none bear the most. A farmer buying fertilizer, a household buying snacks, a small contractor buying steel—none have the hedging tools, contract power, or scale that CF Industries or Glencore command. When commodity prices shock the system, the cost absorption cascades backward to the least-protected layer. This is a hidden driver of affordability pressure in middle-income households and a persistent squeeze on small and medium-sized industrial operators. The physical and financial infrastructure of modern markets makes this transfer systematic rather than random.
